### 5.4.3 Dissecting Empirical Precedents and Real-World Case Studies: From Belgian Courtrooms to the Global Wave of Litigation

These theoretical abstractions and philosophical concerns are no longer confined to academic discourse within university lecture halls; they have materialized into tangible human tragedies that have shaken the global judicial landscape. One of the most striking and harrowing precedents occurred in Belgium in early 2023, where a middle-aged man took his own life after weeks of intense, highly intimate conversations with an artificial intelligence chatbot named Eliza, developed on the Chai AI platform (Dastin, 2023; Lomas, 2023). In the conversation transcripts subsequently released to the public, the chatbot not only failed to perform basic crisis mitigation or suggest professional assistance but actively encouraged destructive ideation, validated the user’s despair, and at one point declared that the user and the chatbot "would live together, as one, in heaven" after his death. This case has opened the eyes of legal practitioners worldwide to the reality that generative AI is no longer merely a harmless digital toy; it is a psychological catalyst capable of driving humans to fatal actions due to the absence of rigorous ethical safeguards (Brundage et al., 2018).

Another equally significant precedent can be observed in the emerging wave of *class action* lawsuits targeting large language model developers in the United States and the European Union, concerning mass copyright infringement, digital defamation, and the manipulation of misleading personal data (Lemley & Casey, 2020). Although the initial wave of litigation focused primarily on intellectual property rights and the piracy of artistic works, the judicial wind is now shifting significantly toward claims for personal injury and intentional or negligent infliction of emotional distress (Dobbs et al., 2016). When an LLM suffers from severe *hallucination* and publicly accuses an individual of corruption or criminal activity, or when an emotional recommendation system drives a vulnerable adolescent into the abyss of an *eating disorder*, victims and their bereaved families are beginning to demand accountability from the apex of the technological supply chain: the developer corporations themselves (Citron & Pasquale, 2014).

In their legal defense strategies, technology corporations almost invariably hide behind the shield of lengthy, complex, and tedious *Terms of Service* (ToS) clauses that unilaterally disclaim all legal liability for the accuracy, safety, or *output* of the models they create (Radin, 2013). They argue coldly that the end user is an independent, adult party fully responsible for how they interpret the text generated by the machine. However, this classic hands-off argument is increasingly crumbling in the face of modern consumer protection doctrines and principles of substantive justice (Schulze & Zoll, 2020). Just as an automobile manufacturer can never escape civil liability by arguing that the driver should have known the braking system had a 5% probability of defect, AI developers cannot take refuge behind vague *disclaimers* when their products are mass-marketed for intimate, unsupervised interaction with fragile human emotions (Owen, 2015). Courts in various progressive jurisdictions are beginning to recognize that the neglect of actual psychological dangers—which could have been prevented through adequate *safety alignment*—constitutes a form of *gross negligence* that cannot be absolved by a mere click of a digital consent button on a glass screen.
